The concern rests entirely on a reading the plan's own sentence forbids, and its "proposed fix" is a restatement of what the plan already prescribes rather than a correction of it.

The plan states the governing invariant, not just three edits. §5.5 (SEMANTIC_CHANGE_GATE_PLAN.md:350-357) opens the passage with "Permissions are derived, never listed:" and then lists the mechanism as one semicolon-joined sentence. Under the concern's literal reading — hook still testing a hardcoded module constant — the five `mcp__isabelle_semantics__*` names would still be *listed*, in `_TOOL_WHITELIST`, for the one path that actually enforces. That reading violates the very clause it is derived from. A plan sentence that names its invariant first and its edits second specifies the invariant; the edits are how it is reached.

2. The closure conversion IS the specification of what the hook tests. Today `_permission_control` is a module-level `async def` (claude_code.py:99-111) precisely because the thing it tests, `_TOOL_WHITELIST`, is a module-level constant (claude_code.py:61-85). It has no other reason to sit at module scope. Moving it inside `_options()` (claude_code.py:436) buys exactly one thing and nothing else: visibility of `self.tools` and of the set derived from it in that scope. If the closure kept testing the module constant, the conversion would be a pure no-op churn edit — and the plan does not contain no-op edits. So plan line 355 ("becomes a closure inside `_options()`") read together with line 355-357 ("`allowed_tools` = mcp__<SERVER_NAME>__<t.name> for t in self.tools plus the built-ins iff cli_tools") already names both the set and the scope in which the hook reads it. The concern's fix — "evaluated once at the top of `_options()` into a local that BOTH `allowed_tools` and the hook closure read" — is a transcription of those two clauses, not a change to them.

3. The severity claim does not survive either half. For the judge session the plan is explicit that a lost verdict is a graceful degradation, not a death: §5.4 step 3 and its "Failures (D10)" paragraph (plan:283-300) say "still no verdict ⇒ CHANGED" and a judge `FatalAgentError` "resolves CHANGED (conservative, converges, today's behaviour) and is written to the host log only". So "the judge's `verdict` is denied the same way" would degrade the gate to today's always-propagate behaviour, not kill a run. For the interpretation session the misimplementation would indeed deny `mcp__isabelle_semantics__answer` — on the very first tool call of the very first session, with `_log.warning("tool denied: %s %s", ...)` (claude_code.py:107) naming the tool. Total, immediate, self-announcing, and impossible to ship past a single smoke run. That is the opposite of a blocker: a blocker is a defect that survives testing or corrupts stored state.

4. The plan's cross-driver claims are already exact against the code, which is what one would check if the derivation were underspecified. `deep_seek.py:178` builds its options via `opts = super()._options()` and only mutates `opts.env`, so a closure created inside claude_code's `_options()` propagates untouched — the plan's "DeepSeek inherits" holds literally. `codex.py:289` already derives its tool set as `want = {t.name for t in self.tools}` — the plan's "Codex derives from `self.tools` already" holds literally. Both checks confirm the author was tracking exactly the derived-set-feeds-every-consumer property the concern says is missing.

The only residue is the name `_TOOL_WHITELIST` for a set that will no longer be the whole allowed set. That is a one-word naming preference on a private module constant, not something that makes the implementation wrong, unsafe, complex or inconsistent — i.e. the kind of finding these ground rules classify as a nitpick.

VERDICT: STANDS (blocker). I reproduced the defect and traced the full path to the crash.

WHAT THE PLAN SAYS. §15.5 `_write` (plan line 923) spells the theorem-alike / persistent branch as

    if not tracked:                              # theorem-alike (deps present) or persistent
        version = (rec.version or w.counter_value()) if e.deps else None     # D15

`rec` here is the record as stored BEFORE this run. §15.3 (plan line 802) defines it: `self.recs = recs or [None] * len(entries)   # the stored record per entry at scan`, and §15.8 step 7 (plan line 1053) hands the task `recs=recs` — i.e. exactly the list `Semantic_DB.get_many(...)` returned, positionally aligned with ALL of the theory's entries. `Semantic_DB.get_many` yields `None` for a key with no record (semantics.py:625-634: `return [self._decode(raw) if raw is not None else None for raw in ...]`). So `rec` is `None` for every entity the store has never seen.

WHY THAT ENTITY SHAPE IS THE COMMON ONE, NOT AN EDGE CASE. A newly added lemma/rule in a WIP theory is: `semantic_digest is None` (semantic_interpretation.py:263-267 — the digest is None for theorem-alike entries, their key's thm128 IS the digest) and `deps` non-empty (the wire builds `deps=[bytes(u) for u in deps]` for every entry, semantic_interpretation.py:1323). So it is untracked in §0's glossary sense but `e.deps` is truthy — the `if e.deps` arm is taken. It has no record, so it is uncached, so it is a seed (§5.2), so it is queued, answered, gated, and reaches `_write`. Every theory being interpreted for the first time is made almost entirely of such entries.

CRASH AND BLAST RADIUS. `None.version` raises AttributeError. It fires inside the open `with Semantic_DB.gate_write() as w:` block. `gate_write` (semantics.py:970-977) is `with self._ensure_env().begin(write=True) as txn: yield ...`, so lmdb aborts the transaction cleanly — no store corruption — but the exception escapes. The `_gate` sketch (plan lines 897-902) catches only `asyncio.CancelledError` and `GateError`; §5.4 (plan lines 296-301) moreover states that a step-5 failure is deliberately re-raised as `GateError`, which "fails the task group and therefore `interpret_file` (session closed, theory not marked)". Either way the run dies and the theory is never marked. Every first interpretation of a theory dies on its first lemma answer.

THE PLAN'S OWN TABLE IS RIGHT; ONLY THE CODE LINE IS WRONG. §3's table row (plan line 97) reads: `| theorem-alike (WIP) | no | answer arrives | stored, else ε | None | eff*(E) |`. "stored, ELSE ε" is precisely the no-record case. The expression `rec.version or w.counter_value()` can express "version is 0/None → ε" but cannot express "there is no record at all". Today's code expresses it correctly and is being replaced by the broken spelling: semantic_interpretation.py:942-947

    if e.semantic_digest is None:
        if e.deps:
            version_to_write[i] = (rec.version if rec is not None and
                                   rec.version else epsilon)

The sibling guard in `_gate` (plan line 885, `if tracked and rec is not None and rec.semantic_digest is not None:`) shows the author knew `rec` is nullable; the `_write` branch simply lost the guard. The UNCHANGED branch's `rec.version, rec.baseline_interpretation` is safe because it is reachable only under that line-885 guard, and the first-write and CHANGED branches never touch `rec` — so this is the single unguarded dereference in `_write`.

WHERE I COULD HAVE PROVEN IT WRONG AND DID NOT. I checked whether `on_answer` might skip the gate for untracked entries (it does not — plan lines 866-876 set `_GATING` and `start_gate(idx)` unconditionally for any first answer), and whether `_write` might receive `rec` already narrowed (it does not — it is called as `_write(task, idx, verdict)`, so it re-derives `task.recs[idx]`).

FIX. Take the concern's second form, not the first: bind the stored fields once at the top of `_write` so no branch can reach a `None` record —

    stored_version  = rec.version if rec is not None else None
    stored_baseline = rec.baseline_interpretation if rec is not None else None

then `version = (stored_version or w.counter_value()) if e.deps else None` and the UNCHANGED branch reads `stored_version, stored_baseline`. That restores today's semantics verbatim and makes the invariant structural rather than remembered, which is the shape this review rewards. Add the missing §10 test case "theorem-alike entry with no stored record ⇒ version = ε, no crash"; §10's current line only says "the theorem-alike and persistent rows (no judge, today's fields)", which a test with a pre-existing record satisfies while leaving this path uncovered.

WHAT IS TRUE. Today the task is built over the todo sub-list only (`entries=[entries[i] for i in uncached]`, semantic_interpretation.py:1175), so `task.results` — the addressing table the tool checks at :592-593 — holds exactly the entries the run asked about, and any other label is rejected as "Unknown entry". §15.8 step 7 (plan:1052-1061) puts ALL entries in the task with non-seed `results` prefilled from the store (§15.8 step 4, plan:1048), so that check can no longer fire for any name of this theory. §15.3's `on_answer` (plan:818-832) branches on `_DONE` and `_GATING` only; a `_NOT_ENROLLED` index falls through to `state[idx] = _GATING; start_gate(idx)`. §5.3.1 (plan:207-231) names five states and never says what an answer for the first one means, and D11 (plan:62) scopes corrections to "an entity already written" — i.e. written *this run* — so no decision of §2 sanctions the fall-through. WHAT IS NOT TRUE, AND WHY THIS IS NOT "MAJOR".

1. "text written for something else" is false. Addressing is exact: `_label` is `(kind title, name)` (:220-229) and `_label_to_idx` routes by it (:615). An answer keyed to entity X carries X's own translation, produced by an agent that has the theory source, the `definition`/`hover`/`desugar` tools and the file path. It is unsolicited, not misdirected. The one way to write X's text onto Y is a kind mislabel colliding with a same-named entry of the guessed kind — and that hazard exists today too, between two todo entries, unchanged by this plan.

2. The only real-world instances support the plan, not the concern. The two "Unknown entry" hits in the host log (~/.isabelle/Isabelle2025-2/log/RPC_attached_1929304-11736284-1788340635153510.log:19189, :181540) are both the agent mislabelling the KIND of an entry that was in its batch ("case-split rule Tree_Set.isin.cases" / "induction rule Binary_Trees.BinTree.induct" for entries listed as `lemma`). Neither is an answer for an entity the run never sent; both still reject under the plan. So there is no observed instance of the posited failure mode.

3. The mint is in the safe direction and inside a settled decision. A non-seed is by construction not stale (its digest matches, its dep keys match, eff\* ≤ interpreted_at, §15.8 step 4), so the fresh text describes the same definition the baseline describes and the expected verdict is UNCHANGED. A mint needs a judge false alarm, measured at 0.8 % (plan:38-41), and D2 (plan:53) settles that "a few needless propagations are acceptable". Crucially, an extra mint over-approximates: §5.3.1's soundness argument fails only if an enrolment is MISSED, never if one is added. So this does not touch §14's soundness rest-point.

4. No stated invariant breaks. "At most once per run" survives, because `on_answer` sets `_GATING` before creating the gate and a second submission then takes the `_GATING`/`_DONE` arm. The completeness invariant is untouched (the slot was already non-None). Termination is untouched (`gates_running` counts the gate, and `_propagate` only enqueues). `_write` (plan:918-942) handles a non-seed record correctly, and the statement refresh it skips (§15.8 step 8, plan:1063-1064) is subsumed by `put_interpretation`'s own `expr=e.prop_str`.

There is no legitimate use for the fall-through — a `_NOT_ENROLLED` entry was never written this run, so it can never be a D11 correction — and the cost of leaving it is a wasted judge session, an overwrite of a stored interpretation by text the agent produced without the entry's rendered statement, provenance hints and locale line (`format_entries`, :499-515), and a small chance of a needless mint and cascade. Against that, the fix is one arm in a loop that already has an `errors` list, and it makes the five-state machine of §5.3.1 total instead of leaving the reader to notice that the tool's address filter no longer carries the policy it accidentally carried before. On this repo's own elegance criterion — a shape that makes the invariant impossible to violate over one that asks people to remember it — that is worth the one line. Severity: minor-to-moderate, not major; a robustness gap, not an unsoundness.

argument:
PARTIALLY STANDS. The mechanical core is real and I confirmed it line by line; the framing ("retries forever", severity major) and the proposed fix are wrong, and the one part that genuinely deserves a change is much narrower than the concern states.

WHAT I CONFIRMED

1. Both throttle arms really do re-enter with `depth` unchanged and really do consume no budget. `semantic_interpretation.py:818-822` catches `ReachLimitError`, sleeps 1200 s and does `return await _run_agent(make_driver, depth)`; `:823-827` catches `RateLimitError`, sleeps 2 s and does the same. The two recycle arms right below them (`:834` and `:855`) both test `depth >= _MAX_AGENT_RECYCLES` and re-enter with `depth + 1`. So the asymmetry the concern points at exists exactly as described, and it is deliberate: the in-code comments say "Throttled, legitimate retry — does not consume the recycle budget."

2. A throttle therefore never reaches the plan's `_judge`. Plan §15.5 lines 913-916 says `_judge` catches `except Exception` and resolves anything it catches to CHANGED. Since neither throttle arm ever re-raises, a throttled judge never produces a verdict; it stays inside `_run_agent`.

3. While that judge is inside a throttle arm, plan §15.4 line 848 (`if not task.gates_running: break`) keeps the interpretation session's `async with make_driver()` block open and, after §8, keeps the interpretation lock held.

4. The concurrency regime really does change. `_BATCH_SIZE = 20` (`semantic_interpretation.py:135`) and `_answer_tool` loops over the whole submitted array (`:585-651`), so one tool call can answer up to 20 entries; under D12 each answer starts its own judge session with no limit, and `schedule_dag` runs theories concurrently at `Multithreading.max_threads ()` (`Tools/semantic_store.ML:1928-1929`). Today at most one `_run_agent` per concurrently scheduled theory can be sitting in the 2 s arm; after this plan it is that plus one per answered-but-ungated entity. The 2 s arm is a fixed interval with no growth and no jitter, so many sessions retry in lockstep — and a 429 is precisely the signal that too many sessions are talking to the API at once. This is the one part of the concern I would actually act on.

WHERE THE CONCERN'S REASONING BREAKS

5. "Retries without bound" is false as written, and I measured it. Both arms re-enter with `return await _run_agent(...)`, which nests coroutine frames rather than tail-calling. I ran a minimal reproduction of that exact shape (raise, sleep, `return await` itself) under the repo's `.venv` python: it dies with `RecursionError` after 991 re-entries at the default recursion limit of 1000. Because the re-entry sits inside an `except` handler, the `RecursionError` is not caught by that same frame's handlers and unwinds the whole chain out of `_run_agent` — where §15.5's `_judge` `except Exception` does catch it and resolve to CHANGED. So a sustained 429 gives roughly 33 minutes of retrying and then a CHANGED verdict, not an eternal hang. A sustained usage cap gives ~991 × 20 min ≈ 13 days, which is unbounded in human terms but not in principle.

6. The run is also interruptible. `Isabelle_RPC_Host/rpc.py:319-338`: when the ML side's socket closes (an Isabelle interrupt), the handler shields the coroutine for a 3 s grace and then cancels it; plan §15.5's `_gate` re-raises `CancelledError`. So "the theory hangs" is really "the theory waits for the quota window or for the user's interrupt".

7. The proposed fix is actively harmful for the usage-cap case, and its premise is wrong. CHANGED is not "free": plan §15.5 `_write` mints a version and `_propagate` (§5.3.1) enrols every theory-internal direct dependent, which the interpretation session must then re-interpret — with the same account that just told us it is out of quota — and the mint propagates to other theories through eff*. Resolving a usage cap to CHANGED converts "wait for the quota window to reopen" into "spend more quota right now", which is the opposite of what the throttle exists for. Waiting out a usage cap is the module's deliberate, documented policy for the interpretation session, and plan §5.4 ("The judge's nested `_run_agent` keeps its own recycle budget") endorses reusing it for the judge. A per-task `throttle_budget` object also adds a field, a subclass override and a re-raise path to make a judge's verdict depend on transient network weather — more machinery, less determinism.

So: the observation about the two arms is correct and worth a small fix aimed at the lockstep, not at the budget. I would call it minor, not major.

(a) `connection.server` is the host process's single `Server`: `Connection.__init__(reader, writer, client_addr, server)` (rpc.py:73-79) and `Server.handle_client` constructing one Connection per accepted socket against `self` (rpc.py:279-282). (b) The plan gives it no reset: `grep gate_emb_store` over the plan hits only lines 1066-1072. §5.6's failure path is "text §12 #4 once, and the prefilter is skipped for the run", and §15.8 implements "skipped" as the attribute being ABSENT. Absence is only true before the first successful run in the host's life; a later run whose startup check fails silently inherits the earlier run's provider, resolved from another Isabelle context's `Semantic_Embedding.embedding_model`. That is precisely what D5 fixes and what §5.6 threads `cfg_context` through `interpret_with_parallel` / `interpret_cone` / `interpret'` to guarantee ("the user's context governs the prefilter (D5)"). The plan establishes the invariant in §5.6 and discards it in §15.8 — an internal inconsistency, not a hypothetical.

(c) The startup check's connection is generally NOT the connection `interpret_file` runs on: each theory's `send_for_interpretation` issues its own `call_command` (semantic_store.ML:1850), and `call_command` pops a pooled connection and returns it on success (RPC.ML:883-895), while a failed heartbeat closes the entire pool (RPC.ML:867-878). The parked `Semantic_Vector_Store` therefore carries `connection=<possibly already closed>`. In the gate path only `store.emb_provider` is used (plan §15.4, line 909), so this is latent rather than immediately fatal — but a process-global object holding a dead per-connection handle is exactly the shape the fix removes.

(d) The registry it re-invents exists and already does the job. `_conn_semantic_vector_store` (semantics.py:2792-2812) resolves the triple through the connection's own config callbacks and returns the cached store; `Semantic_Vector_Store.__init__` registers itself under `canonical_model` in `connection._semantic_vector_stores` (semantics.py:1988-1998); `canonical_model = model` (semantic_embedding.py:284), so the cache key matches and a repeat call hits the cache rather than the "already registered on this connection" raise; LMDB envs are memoized globally by path (semantic_embedding.py:1048-1065), so per-connection stores cause no double-open. The package states the very rule the plan breaks at semantics.py:130-133 ("Cached per CONNECTION, not module-level: one RPC host serves a whole fleet of Isabelle processes"). And the exact call shape the fix needs is already in the file: `_embed_all_missing` does `store = await connection.semantic_vector_store()` inside an RPC handler (semantics.py:2874-2880).

One nuance where the concern overstates severity: a wrong-model prefilter cannot by itself yield UNCHANGED, since D2 requires the judge's explicit "same" AND sim >= 0.90. The damage is a weakened backstop plus needless CHANGED propagation (the 0.90 threshold was calibrated on one model's cosine scale), not a direct route to a missed change. argument:
The concern rests on three factual claims, and all three fail against the plan and the code.

(1) "Process-global state shared by concurrent runs." True that one `Server` serves every connection (rpc.py:73-79, :279-282) — but a live interpretation run is *process-globally exclusive* in that host, by the plan's own §8. The interpretation lock is `filelock.FileLock(<semantic_DB_dir()>/INTERPRETATION_LOCK_NAME, timeout=0, thread_local=False)` (§8.1, plan:470-478), its scope is the database directory (§8.3, plan:538), and `interpret_with_parallel` — the only entry to any live run, including `_auto_embed`'s and `by aoa`'s via `make_interpret_theory_callback` — is wrapped at its definition (§8.2, plan:530-537). Crucially, `semantic_DB_dir()` is resolved from the **host process's** environment (Isabelle_RPC/Isabelle_RPC_Host/paths.py:31-47), so every connection this host serves — the whole fleet the semantics.py:125-133 comment is about — necessarily contends on the *same* lock file, and §8.1 states two instances in one process exclude each other. A second run cannot enter while a first holds it: it takes the D8 arm and skips or errors. So there is exactly one writer and one set of readers of `server.gate_emb_store` at a time. That is precisely why the slot may be a single global one: the "run" it is scoped to is a mutual-exclusion region of the host process.

(2) "No reset, so a failed later run inherits the previous run's provider, contradicting D5." The plan says the opposite in two places. §15.8 (plan:1066-1069): "`interpret_file` receives the resolved `Semantic_Vector_Store` (**or `None`**) through the connection: the startup RPC stores it on the connection's server object **for the run**". §5.6 (plan:387-388): "Failure ⇒ text §12 #4 once, and the prefilter is skipped **for the run**". A failure that leaves a usable store in the slot would not be "the prefilter is skipped for the run", so the check writes the outcome — store or `None` — every run. The "a missing attribute means not checked" clause covers the only remaining case: an `interpret_file` reached without a startup check at all (an older ML, a hand-called RPC), and it fails safe to `None`. D5 therefore holds: the store in the slot was resolved this run, from this run's `cfg_context`, which §5.6 threads from `interpret_with_parallel` precisely because `send_for_interpretation`'s locally rebuilt context "would read the default" (semantic_store.ML:1813-1817).

(3) "It re-invents the per-connection registry." It does not — it *uses* it. §5.4 step 2 (plan:283-286) says the store is "the `Semantic_Vector_Store` the startup check resolved once per run through `await connection.semantic_vector_store()` (semantics.py:2792-2811)". The existing registry does the resolving and the caching; the server attribute only carries the resulting object across connection boundaries, because a run legitimately spans several pooled connections (RPC.ML:883-895 releases the connection per command) and the registry's scope — the connection — is not the run's scope. Handing the result across is not a competing registry.

The connection-lifetime half is inert by the concern's own admission: the gate touches only `task.emb_store.emb_provider.embed(...)` (§15 gate pseudocode, plan:906-908), and `emb_provider` is built by `make_embedding_provider(driver, base_url, model, api_key)` and holds no connection. Nothing in the gate path reads `store.connection`, so a pooled or heartbeat-closed connection on the object is harmless. And `emb_store` is read once, at `InterpretationTask` construction (§15.8 step 7, plan:1046-1049), so it is not even re-read across a theory's life.

The proposed fix is also not free, and collides with a settled decision. `_conn_semantic_vector_store` calls `await _resolve_embedding_config(self)` *before* consulting its cache (semantics.py:2803-2810), so "resolve on my own connection per theory" costs three ML config-lookup round trips per theory, and in the un-configured default case — the case §12 #4 exists for — `_resolve_embedding_config` warns with the full setup text before raising (semantics.py:2772-2779) and never caches the failure, so every theory of the cone would re-print it. D16 (plan:67) was decided expressly so "the hint appears once"; `Connection.semantic_vector_store` has no `warn` knob to suppress it. The plan's shape resolves once and reports once, which is the decision.

One residual window is real but already approved and strictly milder than what it accompanies: §8.1's release-ordering paragraph (plan:481-494) records that after an ML interrupt a cancelled handler's residue may still run past a second run's lock acquisition. In that window a residual gate would prefilter with the new run's provider. The plan already accepts residue that can run a *minting* `gate_write` there and records the surviving corner in `doc/invalidation_limitations.md`; a prefilter under a different model is weaker than that — per D2 (plan:47) the prefilter is optional in the first place ("the judge decides alone" when it cannot be computed), and its only unilateral action is forcing CHANGED, the conservative direction.

The concern bundles four claims of very different strength. Two of them I can refute; one is a fair consistency point; one survives outright, and it survives for a reason the concern itself under-states.

WHAT I CAN REFUTE.

(b) the stalled-retry warning and (c) the give-up failure text. Both sentences understate rather than mislead after the widening, and half of the change the concern attributes to §15.8 item 7 is not attributable to it at all. The numerator of both moves from theory-wide to batch-scoped because of the queue itself — §5.3 says in as many words that "today's theory-wide retry loop … re-scoped to the batch", and §15.4 spells the numerator as `task.unanswered_in_batch()`. That is D12/D13 machinery, settled, not the ALL-entries task. What item 7 changes is only the denominator, and in the give-up case it changes it to the *more* correct value: the very same `_msg_unanswered` also backs the completeness backstop at semantic_interpretation.py:1241-1245, whose contract is "every entry of the theory has an interpretation, or raise" (the invariant comment at :1226-1240), and for that caller `len(task.entries)` over all entries is exactly right — today it is right only because the task happens to hold the todo set. A text that reads "left 3 of 244 entities uninterpreted" is true, non-alarming and points at the theory the user must re-run. I would not spend an approval round on it.

(d) the three per-theory opening lines (:1153-1162). This is a fair point but it is smaller than "the plan leaves it to the implementer". §13 step 8 says: "Texts (§12: find the sites by searching for the dry run's `n`, not by line number)". The dry run returns `len(uncached)` at :1141 and the middle opening line prints `len(uncached)` at :1158 — the same variable, in the same function, twelve lines apart. An implementer following step 8's own instruction lands on these lines. So the plan does route the implementer there; what it does not do is supply the wording, and by the plan's own rule ("§12. User-visible texts — all approved") a user-visible text needs approval. That is a §12 completeness gap, not a design error: the fix is mechanical, the wording already exists in §12 #8–#11 ("at least <n>"), and §5.2 already establishes the lower-bound discipline these lines need. Note also that the zero branch at :1153-1155 ("all N entities are already interpreted … nothing to ask") stays exactly true: §5.2 makes the seed count exact at zero (no seed ⇒ no gate ⇒ no mint ⇒ no enrolment), so only the two non-zero branches need "at least".

WHAT SURVIVES.

(a) the per-answer progress line at :627-635. Here the concern is right, and understates the damage. §15.2's `enqueue` is specified as "results[key] = None; state = _QUEUED; append" — it *un-fills* a prefilled non-seed. The line at :635 recomputes `total_answered = sum(1 for v in task.results.values() if v is not None)` from scratch on every answer. So with the task widened to ALL entries (§15.8 item 7), the counter is not merely rebased onto a denominator dominated by cached entries: it runs BACKWARDS. In a 244-entry theory with 14 seeds it starts at 231/244, can reach "244 of 244 done." while gates are still in flight, then drop to 243/244 the moment one CHANGED verdict enrols a dependent, then print "244 of 244 done." a second time. A progress line that reports completion and then retreats from it is worse than an uninformative one, and this is the line whose own comment at :632-634 calls it "The only fine-grained sign of life during a long theory". §15.8 item 7's "The larger `results` dict costs nothing noticeable" is a claim about storage that the plan lets stand as a claim about consequences generally; §12 never mentions this line, and §12's own tail disposes only of the answer tool's *reply to the agent* ("the `answer` tool's batch-complete reply") as not user-visible — the `_report` line beside it is user-visible and was simply missed, so this is an oversight rather than a deliberate exclusion. §9 does not cover it either.

I also reject the concern's proposed fix, on the plan's own elegance criterion. It asks for "an explicit work denominator" field on `AgentTask` with a `_DONE` numerator. A `_DONE` numerator is wrong: at the moment the answer tool prints, the entity it just recorded is `_GATING`, not `_DONE` (§15.3 `on_answer` sets `_GATING` and starts the gate), so the line would lag every answer by a whole judge session — 8–20 s per D3. And a separate counter field is a second source of truth that `enqueue`, `on_answer`, `_write` and `_propagate` must all remember to maintain. §15.2 already gives the task `self.state`, which is the single source of truth for exactly this; deriving both numbers from it makes the skew impossible rather than merely discouraged.

PARTIALLY STANDS. Two halves, and they do not fare the same.

HALF 1 — "the invariant tests `results` but its comment claims durability" — STANDS as a documentation/shape defect, but NOT as the reachable soundness hole the concern describes.

The comment part is simply true. Under D14 (plan:65) nothing about an entity is on disk until its gate's step 5, so `task.results[key] is not None` no longer implies "on disk". The file will nonetheless keep two comments asserting the retired property: semantic_interpretation.py:602-608 ("PERSIST FIRST, MARK IN MEMORY SECOND … This way 'answered' means 'durable'") and :1228-1240 ("COMPLETENESS INVARIANT … interpret_cone marks a theory interpreted as soon as interpret' RETURNS"), whose test at :1241 is `answered < len(task.entries)` over `task.results`. `interpret_cone` does mark unconditionally (Tools/semantic_store.ML:2010-2012, `val _ = mark_interpreted thy` right after `interpret'`). The plan explicitly says the invariant is "unchanged" (line 209-211 and 861-864) and §11's documentation list (lines 614-634) does not mention either comment. In this file the comments are load-bearing, so shipping one that asserts the opposite of what the code does is a real defect. It is also internally inconsistent: the plan has ALREADY moved the retry loop's notion of "unanswered" to the state machine (`unanswered_in_batch` = state == `_SENT`, plan:766) while leaving the final certificate on `results`.

The reachable-gap part does NOT reproduce. `asyncio.TaskGroup.create_task` (Python 3.12.3, verified from `asyncio/taskgroups.py`) raises in exactly three cases, and I walked each:
 - `not self._entered`: impossible, `interpret_file` enters the group before starting the agent (§15.1, §15.4).
 - `self._aborting` (the concern's "a sibling gate just raised `GateError`"): reachable — the answer-tool handler does run in a foreign task (Claude path: `claude_agent_sdk/_internal/query.py:236-239` spawns each control request with `spawn_detached`; Codex/DeepSeek path: uvicorn/ASGI request task, mcp_server.py:104-116), so it is not cancelled with the parent and can indeed hit `create_task` while the group aborts, with the RuntimeError swallowed into `errors` at :616-622. But the same `GateError` fails the group: `_on_task_done` cancels the parent, `CancelledError` is a `BaseException` and so passes through every handler at :811-862 (none catches `BaseException`), and the group's `__aexit__` re-raises the `GateError`. `interpret_file` therefore raises, `interpret'` never returns, `mark_interpreted` never runs. The entry left answered-but-unwritten is exactly crash shape (i) of §6.4 and is re-listed by the next scan. So no theory is ever marked over a missing record on this path.
 - `self._exiting and not self._tasks` (the concern's "a late correction turn after the loop broke"): unreachable, because the driver session is closed by `_run_agent`'s own `async with make_driver()` (:756, kept in §15.4) before the group's `__aexit__` is reached, so no tool call can arrive afterwards.
The `gates_running`-leak hang is likewise not reachable: it only occurs in the aborting case, where the parent has already been cancelled out of `wait_for_progress`.

HALF 2 — "a per-item write failure now discards the whole theory's paid-for answers" — REFUTED, on two counts.
 (a) `gate_write` is a contextmanager that opens ONE write transaction per call (semantics.py:970-977, `with self._ensure_env().begin(write=True) as txn: yield ...`), and §15.5 uses one `gate_write` per entity. Gates commit as they finish, so a `GateError` loses only the answers still in flight (the `_GATING` ones) — precisely §6.4 crash shape (i). Already-written entities are non-stale for the next scan (§15.8 step 4), so the next run re-asks only the lost ones. "The whole theory's paid-for answers" is not what is discarded.
 (b) The concrete failure class the :602-608 comment was written for — a lone UTF-16 surrogate crashing msgpack's strict-UTF-8 `packb` — is already prevented BEFORE any write by the strip at :601-606, which lives in the tool body that §15.1 carries over wholesale into `mk_answer_tool` (":577-651"). Adding a `msgpack.packb` round trip in `on_answer` (the concern's fix (c)) would re-invent validation for a failure the strip already removes; the remaining write failures (map full, decode error) are not fixable by re-asking the agent, so routing them to `GateError` is the D10-correct behaviour, not a regression. I recommend rejecting (c).

Two claims are bundled. The first (step 3 is unimplementable) is refuted; the second (the step-4 intermediate can lose invalidation signal) is true only in a narrower case than stated, and by a different mechanism, so it deserves one caveat sentence — not the restructuring proposed.

(a) "After step 3 there is no channel from the scan to the write" — REFUTED. `inv_fields` is not the channel; it is a redundant parallel array over the one channel the plan actually uses, `recs`/`rec_cache`. Today's scan already materialises both: `recs = Semantic_DB.get_many(...)` (semantic_interpretation.py:922) and `rec_cache` (:981-982), and phase 1 writes each mint back INTO `recs` in place — `recs[i] = rec = rec._replace(semantic_digest=..., deps=..., version=v)` (:957-959). So after a scan-time mint, `recs[i].version` IS the scan's minted version. §15.3 gives `InterpretationTask` exactly that parameter (`recs: list[SemanticRecord | None] | None = None`, plan:802) and §15.5's `_write` reads `rec = task.recs[idx]` and `ia = eff_star(task, e)` over `rec_cache` (plan:881, 934). In the step-3 tree (scan unchanged, still minting) the implementer replaces `inv_fields=[...]` at :1177-1178 with `recs=[recs[i] for i in uncached]` at the same call site; nothing else is needed. That is precisely why the plan deletes `inv_fields` in step 3 rather than step 5: one source of truth for a record's fields (the record) instead of a second per-index tuple list that must be kept 1:1 with `entries` — the elegance criterion, not an oversight.

Moreover, even if the implementer follows §15.5's `_write` literally in step 3, the no-verdict branch takes `version = w.counter_value()` = ε = the current counter (semantics.py:547-557: `counter_value` returns the last minted value). ε ≥ any version the scan just minted, so the step-3 write can only OVER-signal, never under-signal; and since the scan is unchanged, its todo set is still today's full closure, so no propagation is needed for correctness anyway. §15.11's "behaviour equals today's" holds; its phrase "the scan's fields" means the fields the scan left in `recs`/`rec_cache`, which after phase 1 include its mints. Nothing here is unimplementable.

(b) "After step 4 the signal is destroyed, not deferred" — PARTIALLY TRUE, and the stated mechanism is wrong. The concern asserts "an unraised version". That is not what the plan's code does: with no gate, `verdict` is None, so `_write` takes the §3 row-1 branch and writes `version = w.counter_value()` = ε = C, the global counter maximum, and `interpreted_at = eff*(E) = C`. So the version DOES rise to the top epoch. Staleness is a strict inequality (plan §4 "E is stale iff eff*(E) > interpreted_at(E)"; code :1124 `stale = eff_v > (rec.interpreted_at or 0)`), and a fresh A is a wall contributing `version(A) = C` (:1002-1010 `_contrib`). So a dependent B is re-listed on the next run iff `interpreted_at(B) < C`. Since C is the last mint anywhere in a database spanning hundreds of theories, that inequality holds for the ordinary dependent, and §15.11's "re-interpreted only on the next run" is then literally correct. The loss case is the residue: B whose stored `interpreted_at` already equals C, i.e. B was re-interpreted after the most recent mint in the whole store — which is exactly the "edit this theory, run interpretation, edit it again" loop a developer is in. There, A's digest is consumed by the write and its version cannot rise above C, so B is never re-listed. That corner is real, and §15.11 states a blanket safety property that is not blanket-true.

The proposed fix, however, does not follow from its own claim. "Keep `inv_fields`/`write_answer` alive through step 4" cannot work: step 4 IS the removal of the scan-time mint (§15.8 item 2, "Phase 1 loses its `txn.put` and `counter_next`"), so `version_to_write` no longer exists and `inv_fields` would carry the stored version — the very "unraised version" the concern objects to. And merging steps 4 and 5 fuses a scan rewrite with the prefilter, the JudgeTask, the decision table, propagation and the snapshot raise into one unreviewable, unbisectable step, against the plan's deliberate decomposition. The plan already says the state is "an intermediate state, not shipped" (plan:1115) and its entire test story runs on an isolated `SEMANTIC_DB_DIR` (§10 opening, §15.10 "over an isolated store"); the only exposure is a developer choosing to spend LLM money on a live run of half-finished code against ~/.cache.

So: no restructuring, one sentence of truth in §15.11.

WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE — the severity. The concern says "the embedding keeps describing text the entity no longer has". For a changed meaning that is impossible. `expr` is display text (parent CHECK_OUTDATE_PLAN.md:91 says so in terms: "expr 字段不可用作变更判定：它是展示文本 ... 重排版假阳性"), and for every kind the change signal strictly dominates it:
- constants: `expr` is only the printed type (semantic_store.ML:704-706), while the digest is the declared type AND the own defining axioms AND the abbreviation body (semantic_digest.ML:413-452, whose comment says outright that a type-only signal "is exactly what the existing `expr` field does" and is not enough). Any material change to a constant is a seed.
- types: the digest covers constructors and the typedef set (semantic_digest.ML:500-544), so a datatype or typedef edit is a seed even though `expr` is the raw command source.
- theorem-alike: the universal key is itself the content digest (semantic_digest.ML:12-18: "A theorem's key already carries a content digest (thm128), so the key itself is its change signal"), so an edited statement arrives as a NEW key — uncached — a seed. A changed lemma statement can never present as "same key, drifted prop_str".
What is left that can drift with a zero quote is exactly the display rendering: a comment or whitespace edit inside a type/class/locale command (`source_at_pos`, semantic_store.ML:708-712), an alpha-renaming in a theorem statement (semantic_digest.ML normalizes binder and variable names away), or a notation/print-context difference. That is cosmetic-sync, not correctness. Note too that the refresh never repairs a stale *interpretation* — it only writes `expr` — so it was never an invalidation mechanism.

"Indefinitely" is also wrong: the cone callback runs `interpret_file` for every unmarked theory of the cone, so the next run with any nonzero quote refreshes every non-written entry of that theory via §5.3.2.

WHAT MUST BE REJECTED — the primary fix. "Keep the statement refresh in the scan on both paths" is wrong on the live path and would undo a deliberate part of the design. Under D13/§5.3.1 a non-seed entry can be enrolled later by a CHANGED verdict and then rewritten in full by `Gate_Writer.put_interpretation` with `expr=e.prop_str` (plan line 935, §15.7), so a scan-time refresh would write the record and invalidate its vector for entries the same run rewrites minutes later. The plan's "after the loop, for every entry this run did not write" is the shape that makes the double write impossible; only the dry branch needs the extra call.

Two supporting claims are also misread. (i) Parent discipline 3 does not treat the statement refresh as an exception: CHECK_OUTDATE_PLAN.md:389-393 permits the scan's *version bump* on a dry run (digest/deps in the same put, discipline 1) and never mentions `expr`. (ii) "Persistent-theory entries are hit hardest" is the weakest part, not the strongest: `update_expr` on a system-resident record copies the FULL record up into the user DB and invalidates its vector (semantics.py:751-777), and a persistent entity's `prop_str` is re-rendered in the *user's* current context — so today's dry run can copy up and re-embed system records merely because the reader's notation differs. Removing that from the read-only quote path is a gain, and it is the one place where the plan's choice is positively better than today.

So: a two-line omission on the dry branch, worth fixing; not a major correctness defect, and not by the route proposed.

argument:
The concern splits into a correctness claim and an elegance claim. The correctness claim is refuted by the plan's own text and by two settled decisions; the elegance claim mostly dissolves once you check what the six "forged" items actually are, and the proposed alternative is not clearly better — it re-implements the give-up ladder the plan reuses.

1) "Delivered as FatalAgentError ... silently reinterpreted as CHANGED ... precisely the failure D10 says must never be hidden." This inverts D10. D10 reads: "a mint happens only on the gate's explicit CHANGED verdict; an outcome the gate could not judge is CHANGED (conservative) and is logged". A TypeError in the pair prompt or a KeyError in the verdict tool is exactly "an outcome the gate could not judge", and the plan does both things D10 demands: it resolves CHANGED and it logs. §15.5 says the catch is "logged at warning"; §5.4's Failures paragraph says the outcome "is written to the host log only"; §12's approved-texts block closes with "Host-log only (never shown): judge session failed; judge gave no verdict for some entries."; §10's test list contains "judge `FatalAgentError` => CHANGED, log only, no recycle". So the behaviour is logged, tested, and the user-visible/host-log split is itself an approved decision — arguing it should be surfaced or narrowed is a re-litigation of D10 plus the §12 text ruling.

2) The direction of the failure is the safe one, by D2. D2: "A few needless propagations are acceptable; a missed change is the outcome to avoid." A swallowed bug in the judge path yields CHANGED for every gated entity, i.e. the run degrades exactly to today's no-gate behaviour (everything propagates) — expensive, never wrong, and loud in the log once per entity. The unsafe direction (a bug read as UNCHANGED) is impossible: UNCHANGED requires `judge.verdict is True`, which only the verdict tool can set (§15.5: "returns UNCHANGED iff `judge.verdict is True`; CHANGED otherwise").

3) "Narrow the `except` to the classes that really are failures" cannot be done, because that set is open-ended by construction. `_run_agent`'s catch-all handler (semantic_interpretation.py:851-862) re-raises the *original* transport/SDK exception after `_MAX_AGENT_RECYCLES`; `ReachLimitError`/`RateLimitError` recurse forever, `PoisonedSessionError` converts to `FatalAgentError`. So the exceptions that can escape a judge session are "FatalAgentError, or any exception a backend SDK can raise". Narrowing to `FatalAgentError` would let a dead network inside one judge fail the gate task group and therefore the whole theory (§5.4: a `GateError` "fails the task group and therefore `interpret_file`") — strictly worse than the conservative CHANGED, and a violation of D2's stated preference. The blanket `except Exception` with `CancelledError` deliberately excluded (§5.4: "`except Exception` only, so a cancellation propagates"; `CancelledError` is a `BaseException` since 3.8) is the correct shape here, and §10 tests both halves ("`CancelledError` propagates and cancels running gates").

4) The "six forged pieces" are not forgeries, one by one:
- `self.enqueue(0)`: the judge has exactly one genuine work item — the entity whose pair must be sent. `next_batch()` returning `[0]` is what makes `build_prompt([0])` the pair prompt. Nothing is faked.
- `judge.results[key] = args["why"]`: `results` is the base's per-entry answer slot, and `why` *is* the judge's textual answer (the plan also logs it). Storing the answer in the answer slot is the intended use, not a trick to appease a loop.
- `judge.state[0] = _DONE`: the answer tool on the interpretation side sets state directly too (§15.3: `self.state[idx] = _GATING`). Both tools mark their entry's state; the judge's terminal state is `_DONE` because no gate follows it. Symmetric, not hand-forged.
- `retry_report -> ""`: §15.2 defines this on the base as a documented contract (`# "" = no line`). It is needed for a real reason: the interpretation task's retry report goes to the *user* through `_report(..., warn=True)` (semantic_interpretation.py:798-801, which calls `Connection.warning`), and §12 rules judge failures host-log-only. A judge that printed "1 of 1 entities still have no interpretation" into Isabelle would be the bug.
- `max_stalled_retries`: the judge's one-round retry is an approved decision (plan header, line 10: "the judge's one-round retry (§5.4 step 3)" approved). Turning a policy constant into a per-task attribute is the ordinary way to express an approved policy difference, not machinery-bending. argument:
The design point stands in full; the hazard the concern uses to motivate it is inert, and I verified that by measurement rather than by argument.

WHAT STANDS. §15.5 (plan:933-934, 939) really does put a record that is in no store into the run's shared `rec_cache`, compute `ia` from it, and then overwrite it with the committed record. The whole reason it must do that is that §15.5 addresses the evaluator through a two-argument wrapper, `eff_star(task, e)` (plan:965), which has no version parameter and can therefore only learn E's just-minted version by finding it in `rec_cache`. But the function that wrapper is "today's ... closure" of already takes the version as an argument — `def eff_value(version, deps)` at semantic_interpretation.py:1084-1090, where `best = version` and the deps walk never touches E's own record at all. So the fabricated record exists purely to smuggle one integer past a signature that already accepts it.

The plan is inconsistent with itself here. §15.8 item 4 (plan:1048) calls the very same relocated evaluator in the direct form — `_EffStar.eff_value(rec.version or 0, e.deps)` — for the scan's staleness test, and §15.5 itself says the class is introduced "so the scan and the gates share one implementation; the code inside is unchanged" (plan:969-971). One of the two shapes is redundant, and it is the one that needs a fabricated record.

There is a second, concrete wart the fix removes that the concern does not mention. §3 row 1 ("first write") fires when the record is ABSENT (`task.recs[idx] is None`, so `rec_cache[key]` is `None`). In that case "provisional record with the new version" cannot be a `_replace` — the implementer must hand-build a whole 15-field `Semantic_DB.Record` (semantics.py:266-369) just so that `eff_star(task, e)`'s version read does not hit `None.version`. Passing ε in directly makes that case disappear.

WHAT DOES NOT STAND. The concern presents two consequences that I could not reproduce:

(a) "the plan never says which reading of the fabricated pair is intended when E is reachable from its own dependencies." The two readings are provably the same value. E is read by `_contrib`'s wall test (semantic_interpretation.py:989-1003) only if E lies on a cycle through its own deps, and there the fabricated version can only change the answer if the version handed in is STRICTLY BELOW E's own stored version. The plan never does that: a CHANGED verdict passes `w.mint()` (> counter ≥ every stored version and interpreted_at, §6.3 invariant), a first write passes ε = `w.counter_value()` (≥ every stored version), and UNCHANGED passes `rec.version` itself, for which the fabrication is the identity. In all three the fabrication is inert.

(b) "the invariant thus depends on two paired assignments straddling a fallible write." Nothing can observe the gap. §15.5's own concurrency paragraph (plan:973-977) is right: `eff_star`, `put_interpretation` and the two cache assignments contain no `await`, so no other gate runs between them; and if `put_interpretation` raises, §5.4 turns it into `GateError`, which fails the TaskGroup and hence `interpret_file` (plan:299-302) — the run dies and takes `rec_cache` with it. The repaired assignment is never load-bearing for correctness.

So this is a simplification/consistency finding of the severity the concern itself assigns (minor), not a latent bug — and worth applying, because it deletes a concept ("provisional record") that §14 (plan:700-702) advertises the design as not having.

argument:
Three sub-claims, and only the middle one survives.

(a) REFUTED — "#4 and #5 are specified onto the host log" is contradicted by the plan's own text and by the code line the plan cites. §5.6 (plan:388-390) says `_resolve_embedding_config` "already warns with the full setup text before raising (semantics.py:2778-2779, deliberately)". That line IS `await connection.warning(msg)` (semantics.py:2778) — the Isabelle-visible channel, the same one `_report(..., warn=True)` uses (semantic_interpretation.py:673). D16 (plan:67) then says the startup check passes `warn=False` "so text §12 #4 is printed once, **not on top of the function's own warning**". There is no "on top of" collision to avoid unless #4 lands on the same user-visible channel that `connection.warning` already uses; on the host log the two would not collide at all. So D16 only parses under the reading the concern says is missing. For #5, §12 is titled "User-visible texts — all approved" and closes with an *exhaustive* host-log-only list: "judge session failed; judge gave no verdict for some entries" (plan:664-665). #5 is a numbered §12 text and is not on that list, so it is user-visible by construction; §15.5's "log, print text §12 #5 once" (plan:911) names two acts, and `_report(warn=True)` is precisely "log, then put in front of the user". Naming `_report` explicitly in §5.4/§15.5 is a one-word editorial improvement, not a defect that would make the implementation wrong.

(b) STANDS, but minor, not major. §5.4 step 2 (plan:268-270) and its Failures paragraph (plan:296-297) say the prefilter is skipped "for the rest of the run", and §12 #5 (plan:653-654) is approved as "(once per run)", where "run" means the cone run (§5.6:382 "once per cone run, in `interpret_with_parallel` before any theory starts"). §15.3:806 implements it as `self.prefilter_disabled = emb_store is None` on `InterpretationTask`, and §15.5:911 sets `task.prefilter_disabled = True`. But §5.1 (plan:139-143) makes one `InterpretationTask` per theory, and theories run concurrently as futures under `schedule_dag`. So "the rest of the run" becomes "the rest of this theory": a dead endpoint costs one failed embed call and one user-visible #5 line per theory in the cone, up to the cone's theory count. This is a spec-vs-blueprint contradiction the implementer must resolve one way or the other, so it is worth fixing — but it is not a correctness bug: D2 (plan:53) makes "prefilter skipped, judge decides alone" a sound outcome, and the blast radius is bounded by theory count, not entity count.

The fix is one line and the plan has already provisioned the home for it: §15.8 (plan:965-972) stores the resolved store at `connection.server.gate_emb_store`, and `Connection.server` is the single per-process `Server` object shared by every connection (rpc.py:79, constructed once at rpc.py:632/664) — i.e. the plan already treats that slot as run-scoped and reads it from each theory's separate connection. Clearing that same slot on the first failed embed call makes "skipped for the rest of the run" and "printed once per run" literally the same fact, with no new scoping hazard beyond the one §15.8 already accepted.

(c) REFUTED, on two independent grounds.

First, it re-litigates a settled decision. §12's footer, "all approved 2026-09-08", puts "judge session failed" and "judge gave no verdict" on the host log deliberately, and D10 (plan:61) already fixes the semantics: an outcome the gate could not judge is CHANGED and is *logged*. The concern proposes a new user-visible line and concedes "wording needs the owner's approval" — that is a request to reopen §12, which this review's ground rules exclude.

Second, the specific scenario is unreachable as described. The concern's own evidence — deep_seek.py:136-140 (missing `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`), :158-163 (hijacked env), :166-176 (missing pricing / context window), codex.py:214-217 (missing pricing), claude_code.py:479-486 (`CLINotFoundError`) — are all `__init__`/`__aenter__` failures that depend on nothing but driver name, model and environment. D3 (plan:54) gives the judge the interpretation driver's *own* driver and model; the judge driver differs only in `system_prompt`, `tools`, `cli_tools=False` and `on_context_reset` (§15.6, plan:1014-1018), none of which any of those raises consults. So an unconstructable judge backend is an unconstructable interpretation backend, which raises `FatalAgentError` at the run's first `make_driver()` and is re-raised unrecycled by `_run_agent` (semantic_interpretation.py:842-848) — the run fails loudly before a single entity is ever gated. And because these raises land before any turn, such a judge costs zero API calls, so "pays a judge session per entity" is wrong for exactly the failure class the concern cites.

The one residual variant — sessions that start but are denied their `verdict` tool, so every gate silently falls to CHANGED at real cost — is the new permission-derivation code of §5.5, and the plan already targets it twice in §10: "`allowed_tools` for a judge driver is exactly the `verdict` name" (plan:611) and the interactive scaffold whose acceptance criterion is "a live run's host log must show judgements" (plan:619-620). §15.9's `judge_` cost breakdown gives a second signal (judge cost accrued with no UNCHANGED verdicts anywhere). Asking additionally for a run-level user-visible degradation banner is a product decision for the owner, not a defect in the blueprint.

The concern rests on three factual claims about the plan and the code; all three are wrong, and its proposed fix, taken literally, introduces the exact memo bug the existing code was hardened against.

(1) "A combination that exists nowhere else, and that `_contrib`'s wall test reads." The pair (new version, pre-run `interpreted_at`) is not novel: it is today's COMMITTED state of a bumped entity for the whole run. Today's scan mints at first visit and puts `rec._replace(semantic_digest=..., deps=..., version=v)` — `interpreted_at` deliberately untouched — into the store and into `recs[i]` (semantic_interpretation.py:952-959), and `rec_cache` is then built from those very records (:980-982). Every eff* of today's run therefore reads exactly this pair, and the eff\* verification (`eff_shield_verification/REPORT.md`, whose prototype "kept today's scan-time mint", plan §4 "Scope of the verification") was measured on it. The reading is also unambiguous and forced: with `ver = new version` and `ia = pre-run`, the wall test `ver > 0 and ia > 0 and e <= ia` (:989-1003) can never hold, because the minted number exceeds every stored number (counter monotone, semantics.py:559-568; plan §6.3 "no stored version or interpreted_at exceeds the counter"), so `e >= ver > ia`. Meaning: "an entity that just minted and has not yet absorbed it is stale and passes its signal through" — the only sound reading, and the one the plan already states in §4.

(2) "The plan never says which reading is intended when E is reachable from its own dependencies." It does not need to, because the two readings coincide. eff*(E) at E's own write is `max(version(E), contributions)`, and every contribution is bounded by the counter (§6.3). After a mint, `version(E) = counter_next` is the largest number in the domain, so eff*(E) = the minted version whatever the cycle hands back. In the UNCHANGED and theorem-alike rows nothing is minted, so the "provisional record" is byte-identical to the record already in `rec_cache`. In the first-write row the version is ε = `counter_value()` (semantics.py:944-950), which again dominates every stored version. I checked each row of the §3 table: the pre-commit assignment cannot change a single written `interpreted_at`. It is a faithful port of today's :958 (keep `rec_cache` in step with the mint), not a fabrication the result depends on.

(3) "The invariant depends on two paired assignments straddling a fallible write." The two assignments straddle nothing observable. §15.5's concurrency paragraph (lines 973-977) and §6.4 fix the shape: `gate_write`'s body is synchronous with no `await` inside (semantics.py:970-975 enforces one write txn), gates are asyncio tasks on one loop, so no other gate can run between line 933 and line 939 — the provisional record is invisible to every other reader by construction. On the failure path the plan is explicit (§5.4 "Failures", lines 296-303): a `gate_write` failure is re-raised as `GateError`, which fails the task group and therefore `interpret_file`; the session is closed and the theory is not marked, and `rec_cache` is per-task in-memory state that dies with the task. §6.4 crash shape (ii) covers the store side: LMDB aborts the transaction, so the record and the counter are untouched. So "rec_cache == store for every later eff\*" (§5.4 step 5, and the docstring already shipped in step 1, semantics.py:952-966) holds for every run that continues, which is the only case in which a later eff* exists.

(4) The premise that the fabrication "exists only because eff_star reads the version out of the cache" also mis-describes why the wrapper exists. `eff_value` today shares one long-lived `memo` (:980) across all per-entry calls of the scan (:1122, :1131) — correct there, because "which digests changed is a fixed fact of this batch" (:924-928). argument:
**(a) The predicted spurious "busy" cannot happen, because the release path is strictly SHORTER than any acquire path on the same event loop.**

The concern is right about the mechanism (release is a side effect of the peer noticing EOF) but wrong about the consequence, and it never counts the hops on the two paths.

First, what the concern feared most is not there: the 3-second grace of rpc.py:326-338 only runs when a `func_task` is in flight when the reader task completes. On the lock connection there is none: `with_interpretation_lock` sends exactly one request (`try_acquire`), `handle_client` writes the reply (rpc.py:349) and loops back to park in `connection.read()` (rpc.py:133) for the entire duration of `body ()`. When ML closes, the handler is idle, so the path to release is: transport sees EOF → reader task raises and puts the sentinel (rpc.py:118-123) → `handle_client`'s `read()` raises `ConnectionResetError` → caught at rpc.py:352 → `return` → `finally` → `connection.close()` (rpc.py:377) → `on_close` → `lock.release()`. No timer, no sleep, no grace.

Second, ML's `close_connection` really does close the socket, not just the ML streams: both `BinPrimIO` records' `close` fields are `close_permissive socket`, i.e. `Socket.close` (RPC.ML:97, :140, :158), so `closeOut`/`closeIn` (RPC.ML:336-337) hand the fd back to the kernel and the FIN is on the wire before the ML command returns.

Now the ordering. For a back-to-back pair of runs in one ML process, the FIN is queued before run 2 exists at all (run 2 only starts after `close_connection` returned, then must do `get_connection ()` and write a request). So the lock connection's EOF is readable at the host in the same epoll batch as run 2's request or an earlier one. If earlier, the lock is already free. If the same batch — the case the concern builds on, "the loop was blocked in synchronous work" — count the callbacks:

- release: transport `_read_ready` (EOF) → reader task resumes, puts sentinel → `handle_client` resumes, and it releases **inline in its own step** (`finally: connection.close()`).
- acquire: transport `_read_ready` (data) → reader task resumes, unpacks, puts → `handle_client` resumes and only *schedules* the procedure, `func_task = asyncio.create_task(func(arg, connection))` (rpc.py:317) → the FileLock is taken one further iteration later.

The acquire pays one extra scheduling hop that the release does not, precisely because the release is done in the handler's own `finally` while every remote procedure goes through `create_task`. So even in the exact tie, and whatever order epoll reports the two descriptors in, the release runs first. There is no interleaving in which run 2 loses the lock to a run whose ML side has already returned.

The "loop regularly blocks in synchronous work" premise also does not apply at that instant. The plan's synchronous blocks (§15.5, "the LMDB writes are synchronous blocks with no `await` inside") happen *during* a run; by the time the lock connection closes, `body ()` has returned, which means the `interpret_file` coroutine already returned its result to ML (§5.1). The host is idle with respect to this run.

The only residue is two runs in two different Isabelle processes on one database, where the two hosts share no event loop. But there the two runs really are simultaneous to within one event-loop turn of an idle loop, and D8 is exactly the decision that such an answer is "busy": §12 #2 and #3 tell the user to wait and run the command again, and #3 states the operating rule ("Two runs must never share a database"). Asking for a sub-millisecond-accurate liveness answer across processes is re-opening D8, not implementing it.

Finally, the proposed fix is a net loss even if the window were real. §8.1 states the design as "No release procedure, no sidecar", and the value of that is that a lock cannot outlive the connection that holds it — the OS enforces it. An explicit `release_interpretation_lock` re-introduces: a procedure that must be idempotent, a "released but still pooled" state on the `Connection`, and an extra round trip inside a *finaliser*, which is the one place where §8.2 is fighting interrupts (the round trip would itself need interrupt protection, and on any failure would have to fall back to closing anyway). More machinery, one more invariant to remember, guarding a window that cannot bite.

**(b) Closing the connection on the `NONE` arm is the safer shape, and the path is not frequent.**

The observation is factually correct: the §8.2 finaliser closes whenever `conn` is `SOME`, including the "lock busy" arm where no lock was taken. But the claimed cost and the claimed frequency both fail.

Frequency: the `NONE`-busy arm fires only when another run genuinely holds the lock. On the `by aoa` / `_auto_embed` path it is reached only after `update_interpretations` has already done a dry run and found `n > 0` (semantics.py:1841-1852) — the dry run is never locked (D8) — and `_auto_embed`'s interpretation step is double-gated and skipped outright by AoA's query path (semantics.py:2120-2122, and the comment at :2110-2117: "AoA passes False on its lookups ... its query path pays nothing here"). So this is an exceptional path, not a hot one.

Cost: one `close_connection` plus, if the pool then empties, one `make_connection ()` — in ephemeral mode a loopback `try_connect` and an identity handshake (RPC.ML:867-878, :776-786). That is microseconds-to-milliseconds, on a path whose whole purpose is to *skip* a run that would have cost minutes and dollars.

Against that, the branch the concern proposes costs an invariant. §8.2 states it in one line: "The connection is never released to the pool: closing it is what releases the lock." That is unconditionally checkable by reading the finaliser. Branching on the acquire outcome makes the finaliser's correctness depend on a flag being right forever, and the failure mode of getting it wrong is the worst one this design has: a connection handed to `release_connection` sits in `connection_pool` (RPC.ML:880-881) and is never closed while the ML process lives, so a lock mistakenly returned to the pool is leaked for the session, with no timeout and — by §8.1's own choice — no release procedure to recover it. The cited precedent does not transfer either: `call_command`'s `normal` flag (RPC.ML:883-895) distinguishes "the protocol round trip completed" from "the connection may be in an undefined state"; it says nothing about ownership of an external resource, and reusing its shape here would need a second, differently-motivated flag.

Trading a permanent-lock-leak hazard for one avoided loopback connect on a rare path is the wrong side of the "make the invariant impossible to violate" rule.

Both halves reproduce against the code as it actually is.

(a) §8.1 (plan 466-491) says in so many words: the FileLock is stored on the Connection, `Connection` gains an `on_close` list "run by `close()`", "the lock module registers the release", "No release procedure, no sidecar" — and §8.2 ends with `try close_connection c`. The release is therefore reachable only through rpc.py's `handle_client` `finally` (rpc.py:374-377), which is reached only after the reader task turns EOF into the `None` sentinel (rpc.py:110-123) and `read()` (rpc.py:139-146) raises on it. `close_connection` (RPC.ML:334-338) returns the instant the ML streams are shut, so `with_interpretation_lock` returns while the lock may still be held. §8.1's "Release ordering" paragraph analyses only the other direction (a cancelled worker handler's residue writing *after* a second run acquired). D8 makes the consequence a hard error (§12 #2/#3), not a wait.

I checked the one thing that could have refuted this — rpc.py's 3 s grace (rpc.py:327-338) — and it does not apply to the lock connection, which sits idle in `connection.read()` with no `func_task` in flight. So the window is a few event-loop turns, not seconds. But the host is single-threaded and its own comments document long synchronous work on the loop (semantics.py:628-634: `_auto_embed` runs `get_many` on the event loop over lists that "can be 10^5 long"; `write_answer`, semantic_interpretation.py:381-402, is a synchronous LMDB put). A mimic that reproduces exactly rpc.py's reader-task -> Queue -> handle_client -> finally -> close chain, with the loop blocked in 50 ms chunks and the next run holding a pooled connection (RPC.ML:867-878), gave 5/200 spurious "busy" acquires (0/200 on an idle loop). That is not a theoretical window.

A second, purely internal confirmation: §10's ML test "interrupt during the acquire round trip leaves the next acquire succeeding" (plan line ~604) is not satisfiable by §8.1's mechanism — after an interrupted round trip the lock may be held and is freed only once the host notices EOF. The plan's own test assumes a synchrony §8 does not provide.

(b) The §8.2 finaliser is unconditional: `(case ! conn of SOME c => (try close_connection c; ()) | NONE => ())`. On the `NONE` arm `try_acquire` returned false, no lock was ever taken, and a healthy heartbeat-good connection is destroyed anyway. `call_command` (RPC.ML:883-895) makes precisely this distinction with a `normal` ref; `release_connection` is already exported (RPC.ML:51). Once the pool drains, `get_connection` falls through to `make_connection ()` -> `ephemeral_connection` -> `validate_attached` (RPC.ML:615-640), i.e. a TCP connect plus an identity round trip through the same possibly-blocked loop. Small, but a gratuitous divergence from the established idiom, which is the "inconsistent with the code as it actually is" bar.

One correction to the concern's own fix: it proposes calling the release *from the finaliser and awaiting the reply*. That is unsafe. `\<^try>… finally` is `Isabelle_Thread.try_finally`, whose finaliser `f ()` runs outside `run` inside `uninterruptible_body` (isabelle_thread.ML:185-187), and `mk_conn` leaves the read timeout `NONE` (RPC.ML:331) — a stalled host would wedge the thread with interrupts disabled. The release call belongs in the body, where it is interruptible.

Severity minor is right: no record is corrupted, and the damage is a spurious error or a skipped automatic update. But the fix is small and removes a "ML's return does not mean the lock is free" hazard that nothing in the plan documents.

fun with_interpretation_lock body =
  let val conn = Unsynchronized.ref NONE
      val no_lock = Unsynchronized.ref false   (*!conn provably holds no lock*)
  in
    \<^try>\<open>
      let val c = Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible (fn run => fn () =>
                    let val c = run get_connection () in conn := SOME c; c end) ()
      in
        if call_command' try_acquire_cmd c ()
        then let val r = body ()
                 val _ = call_command' release_cmd c ()
                 val _ = no_lock := true
             in SOME r end
        else (no_lock := true; NONE)
      end
    finally
      (case ! conn of
         SOME c => if ! no_lock then release_connection c else (try close_connection c; ())
       | NONE => ())\<close>
  end

`no_lock` is true only on the two arms where ML has a positive answer that no lock is held (acquire returned false; release acked). Every unknown outcome — acquire raised, body raised or was interrupted, release raised — leaves it false, so the connection is closed and `on_close` frees the lock as today. Both good arms now hand the connection back to the pool, which fixes (b) for free. Give `release_cmd` a finite `timeout` (call_command' honours `#timeout`, RPC.ML:535-541) so a wedged host cannot stall the release.
